rows: The inference design cannot produce a significant result. With six paired folds, five comparisons per horizon and a Holm correction, the smallest attainable two-sided exact Wilcoxon p value is 0.03125, which becomes 0.156 after correction, so no effect of any size can reach 0.05. The statement that none of the fifteen comparisons was significant is therefore an arithmetic certainty rather than an empirical finding, and it cannot support the sentence in the abstract about fold-level inference. Move the primary inferential unit to the day and spatial-block clusters, otherwise state plainly that the study is underpowered and drop the stability conclusion altogether.

The three horizons differ in the completeness rule and not only in window length. Table 3 requires one of one observed hour at the shortest horizon, three of three in the middle and at least five of six at the longest, so the six hour target can be an average over five hours with the gap anywhere inside the window, which is a different quantity from a mean over consecutive hours. The manuscript discusses the window-length effect carefully but says nothing about the missing hour. The consequence is visible in the sample audit, where the middle horizon keeps fewer test cases than the longest, 24805 against 29141, even though its window is shorter. Please report how many long-horizon targets are computed from five hours rather than six, and discuss whether those cases behave differently from the complete ones.

The treatment of missing data contradicts the central argument. The planned grid contains 403512 slots and only 241601 records come back, so the slot-level return rate is 59.87 percent and roughly forty percent of planned positions never produce data. Section 3.3 and Fig. 2 report a daily availability of 97.30 percent, and that denominator is never defined and never reconciled with 59.87 percent. Worse, everything absent is recorded as missing while only the 1170 returned records below the confidence cut are treated as ineligible, after which forward filling and training-period medians are applied. This assumes that absence is unrelated to speed, while commercial floating car data are missing precisely at night, at low volumes and where probe coverage is thin, so a missingness analysis and an imputation sensitivity study are both needed.

Nothing in the paper operationalises reliability. The target is the speed returned by the provider, not radar, not loop detectors and not a synchronised reference, as Section 5.7 concedes. The experiment therefore speaks to the temporal predictability of a commercial traffic product rather than to whether sparse floating car data can forecast real speeds. There is also no probe vehicle count, no sampling rate and no penetration rate, so the source of the sparsity is unknown. The title should be changed to match what was actually measured.

The most important family of models is absent. Three of the six models are naive baselines, and the spatio-temporal architectures cited in the related work, including the transformer and the convolutional-recurrent models, are never run. Every hyperparameter is frozen, with a fixed ridge penalty, a fixed boosted model of 500 trees and a single-layer recurrent model of 64 units, and no validation-based tuning is performed, so the weak showing of the recurrent model cannot be separated from an insufficient capacity and an insufficient training budget. Further, the related work on time-series forecasting, uncertainty-aware prediction, and heterogeneous feature integration could be expanded slightly. Studies such as Separating the Predictable Part of Returns with CNN-GRU-Attention from Inputs to Predict Stock Returns, Enhancing Stock Ranking Forecasting by Modeling Returns with Heteroscedastic Gaussian Distribution, and A Hierarchical Deep Model Integrating Economic Facts for Stock Movement Prediction may provide useful perspectives on temporal feature learning, uncertainty modeling, and the integration of contextual information. A brief discussion of these methodological insights could help better contextualize the forecasting models and reliability analysis considered in this study.

The boosted model reaches 0.949 against 0.950 for persistence and 0.961 for the seasonal baseline, differences of about 0.1 to 1.3 percent, and the abstract reports only the winner while omitting that the three are effectively tied. Several writing and figure issues should be fixed. In the abstract, the phrase challenging where fixed roadside sensing is sparse uses where for a condition. Section 5.6 writes approximately distributed between two bounds, which is not idiomatic. Section 5.1 mixes the present tense with a past perfect in one sentence. The text refers to seven traffic-state and reliability descriptors while Table 2 lists eight non-calendar features, and Table 2 itself notes that the third feature is numerically identical to the second. Section 3.1 says the nodes are numbered along the mainline while Section 5.6 says there is no verified distance coordinate. Fig. 4 places errors from three different window lengths on one axis, and Fig. 5(d) uses a node index that the text says is not a distance axis, so both figures should be redrawn. Table 5 has no per-fold sample sizes, Table 7 supports the percentage claims without intervals and without per-fold values, and the multiple-comparison correction is cited to a psychology methods paper rather than to the original Holm paper. None of the twenty-one references is a standard traffic forecasting benchmark dataset, which sits oddly with the evaluation framing.

Considering that the entire evaluation is based on only 51 observation nodes along a 130-km highway corridor and approximately three months of data, the general applicability of the proposed framework remains uncertain. What evidence suggests that the reported model rankings would remain consistent across highways with different traffic densities, road geometries, and seasonal conditions? It would be important to test the framework on additional corridors and longer observation periods, preferably including both congested urban highways and rural roads, to determine whether the findings reflect general forecasting behavior rather than characteristics of this particular dataset. Could such validation be provided?

A major concern relates to the selection of usable observations. The paper reports that the hourly data coverage is 82.71% under the primary 2-of-4 rule, whereas the coverage increases to 96.12% under the 1-of-4 rule and decreases to only 15.70% under the 4-of-4 rule. These differences suggest that the selected completeness threshold substantially changes the available dataset. Would the authors provide a detailed sensitivity analysis showing how all six forecasting models perform under these alternative thresholds? More importantly, could the excluded observations be associated with congestion or other difficult traffic conditions, potentially producing overly favorable prediction errors?

The authors improved their ML model by using causal missing-data imputation with historical traffic and reliability features, and averaging XGBoost predictions across three random seeds. This is great; however, apart from these techniques, reducing dataset Kolmogorov complexity (the shortest program to produce the output) can also improve model accuracy, as seen in studies leveraging decreased complexity for rapid accuracy gains (e.g., https://doi.org/10.1007/s10462-019-09750-3; https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-023-28763-1). Please read and reference these two papers.

With only six folds serving as the main statistical units, the evidence supporting differences between forecasting models appears particularly weak. XGBoost improves upon SeasonalHA by approximately 1.2%, 2.8%, and 2.9% across the three horizons, yet none of the 15 statistical comparisons is significant after correction. Furthermore, the supplementary day-by-spatial-block analysis reverses the signs of the XGBoost and SeasonalHA differences. Can the authors explain how these conflicting estimates affect the interpretation of model superiority? Additional independent evaluation periods, uncertainty estimates, and an assessment of whether such small improvements have practical value would be necessary to support the conclusions.

The GATE-FCD "framework" is mostly standard good practice: rebuild the full time grid, fit scalers on training data only, fill missing values causally, and test every model on the same cases. Giving it an acronym doesn't make it a contribution. The title asks whether sparse FCD can reliably forecast highway speeds, but the paper never says what reliable means, so the question goes unanswered.

The statistics can't find a difference even if one exists. With six folds, the smallest p-value a Wilcoxon test can give is 0.031. Holm over five comparisons turns that into 0.156, which is exactly the number that keeps appearing in Figure 6. It even shows up for Persistence vs HA at H1, where the gap is almost 0.9 km/h. So "nothing was significant" was decided by the design, not the data. Please use something with real power, such as Diebold-Mariano on daily loss differences or many more rolling origins.

I'd also like to know what the target actually looks like. An MAE under 1 km/h and an sMAPE around 1% on a highway suggest the speed sits near free-flow almost all the time. Please show its distribution, how often current speed equals free-flow speed, and how the confidence values are spread. TomTom fills low-confidence periods partly from historical profiles, and you keep records down to 0.80. That may be why SeasonalHA is so hard to beat. Add a free-flow baseline, and report errors separately for congested periods, since that is where a forecast is useful. The road-closure filter and the fully-observed target rule may be removing exactly those periods.
